faqs.question: How do I start a my favourite festival Diwali essay?
faqs.answer: Name Diwali as your favourite festival in the first sentence, then say which part of it you mean, such as one lamp, one meal or one person. A marker should know your topic and your focus before the second sentence.

faqs.question: Should a favourite festival essay be written in the past tense or the present tense?
faqs.answer: Use the past tense for the one Diwali you are retelling and the present tense for what happens every year. All three model essays on this page mix the two in exactly that way.

faqs.question: Is it okay to invent details in a my favourite festival essay?
faqs.answer: No. It is a recount, so the strongest details are the ones you remember, and teachers can usually tell an invented scene from a lived one. The neighbours and plates in the models are invented only because they are models.

faqs.question: Will my teacher accept one of these model essays as my own work?
faqs.answer: It should not be handed in as yours. They are labelled models to read and learn from. Use their structure, one scene, a second voice and an ending about what changed, with your own Diwali in it.

faqs.question: How many paragraphs should a 250-word essay on my favourite festival have?
faqs.answer: Four or five short paragraphs is a good fit for 250 words. The 250-word model here uses five: an opening, three scenes from one afternoon and a closing promise.

faqs.question: How are the words in a school essay counted?
faqs.answer: Most teachers count every space-separated word, including small words such as a and the. The models on this page were counted that way: 150, 250 and 400 words exactly.

faqs.question: Which date should I write for Diwali 2027 in my essay?
faqs.answer: Write Friday, 29 October 2027: Diwali (Lakshmi Puja) falls on Friday, 29 October 2027, according to Drik Panchang's New Delhi calendar, though Tamil Deepavali is listed a day earlier. Diwali 2026 falls on Sunday, 8 November 2026.

faqs.question: How do I end a favourite festival essay without a cliché?
faqs.answer: End on what you now understand or plan to do, tied to your own scene. A line such as lighting the first diya yourself this year is stronger than a general line about good defeating evil.

faqs.question: Can I write about Diwali as my favourite festival if my family is Jain or Sikh?
faqs.answer: Yes. Jains mark Diwali for Mahavira's nirvana and many Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas on the same night, so write the version your family keeps.

faqs.question: Will SubhSandesh write my Diwali essay?
faqs.answer: No. SubhSandesh makes personal greeting pages and does not write or check school work. Its Diwali card is for wishing one person after your essay is finished.

article.contentMarkdown:
# My Favourite Festival Diwali Essay: 150, 250 and 400 Words in First Person

A "my favourite festival Diwali essay" works best as a true first-person story about one Diwali moment, not a general report on the festival. Below are three original model essays of exactly 150, 250 and 400 words, each built on a single scene, with the 2027 date checked: Diwali falls on Friday, 29 October 2027.

They are models to learn from, not to submit. SubhSandesh builds greeting pages, not homework, but our data says something about revising: across 1,396 apology pages the median gap from first save to last edit is 2.5 hours, and 90.9% of started pages are finished and shared (September 2026).

## What makes a "my favourite festival" essay different from a Diwali essay?

A Diwali essay explains the festival; a "my favourite festival" essay is a recount of what happened to you. A [2016 study of third graders' story writing](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC4761367) found most children made small fixes as they typed but few went back to revise earlier text, and revision activity helped explain story quality.

It logged typed stories, not Indian classrooms, so read it as a pointer rather than proof. The pointer is simple: rereading and fixing a draft is part of what makes a story good.

## Model 1: my favourite festival Diwali essay in 150 words (Classes 3–5)

This one stays with a single diya and a single neighbour. That focus keeps 150 words from feeling thin.

**Model essay, 150 words. Read it, then write your own.**

> My favourite festival is Diwali, and my favourite part of it is one small clay lamp. Every year my mother hands me the diya for the staircase landing outside our flat, and it is my job alone.
>
> Last Diwali I filled it with mustard oil, pressed the cotton wick down and lit it just after sunset. The wind in the stairwell kept bending the flame, so I cupped my hands around it while my little brother fetched a steel glass to shield it. It stayed alight until we finished the Lakshmi puja inside.
>
> Later our neighbour from the second floor stopped on the landing. She said our lamp was the first thing she saw as she climbed the stairs, and I felt as proud as if I had lit the whole building.
>
> That is why I love Diwali so much. Even one small light, guarded carefully, can welcome somebody home.

## Model 2: my favourite festival Diwali essay in 250 words (Classes 6–8)

The middle model follows one afternoon job across six homes. It adds other people's voices and a promise at the end.

**Model essay, 250 words. Read it, then write your own.**

> Ask me to name my favourite festival and I will say Diwali before you finish the question. I love the lamps and the rangoli, but what I wait for all year is one job that belongs only to me: carrying sweets to our neighbours.
>
> On Diwali afternoon my grandmother arranges kaju katli, besan laddoo and her own crisp shakarpara on six steel plates. She covers each plate with a cloth napkin and sends me off with a warning not to taste anything on the way. I climb up all four floors of our building, ringing one doorbell after another.
>
> Our building has an unwritten rule: no plate comes back empty. Mrs Fernandes on the first floor always promises to return mine "with interest", and by evening it arrives carrying plum cake. Rizwan uncle sends coconut barfi, and the Gill family sends pinni wrapped in foil.
>
> When the sun sets, we light diyas along the balcony and sit together for the Lakshmi puja. Later I lie on the sofa, too full to move, counting how many kitchens I tasted in a single day. Every year the answer is six, and every year I feel that the festival has grown bigger than our own flat.
>
> Diwali teaches me that a celebration grows when you carry it out of your own door. This year I am going to ask my grandmother for a seventh plate, because a new family moved into the ground floor in June and nobody has rung their bell yet.

## Model 3: my favourite festival Diwali essay in 400 words (Classes 9–10)

The longest model has a turning point: something goes wrong and the writer changes their mind. It carries two checkable facts.

**Model essay, 400 words. Read it, then write your own.**

> Diwali is my favourite festival, and the Diwali I remember most clearly is the one when the electricity failed. I had always thought of it as a festival of bright bulbs and loud evenings, but that night taught me what the lights are really for.
>
> The preparations began a week early. My mother and I washed the curtains and cleared the cupboards, my father climbed a ladder to hang strings of LED lights along the balcony, and my sister and I drew a peacock rangoli at the front door with coloured powder, which took us almost two hours. On the evening itself we wore new clothes and gathered in the prayer room for the Lakshmi puja.
>
> Just after seven o'clock, as my father began the aarti, every light in our colony went out at once. The LED strings, the ceiling fan and the television all fell silent together. Somebody downstairs groaned, a child started crying, and for a moment our festival seemed to be over.
>
> Then my grandfather asked us to bring every clay diya in the house. We found thirty-one, filled them with oil and placed them along the balcony, the stairs and the window ledges. Within minutes the families around us were doing the same, and our street glowed the way it must have looked long before anyone owned an electric bulb.
>
> Sitting by the lamps, my grandfather told us how the people of Ayodhya lit rows of lamps to welcome Rama home after fourteen years of exile. I had heard that story every year, but in the dark it finally made sense to me. He did not need a single bulb to tell it, and none of us reached for a phone.
>
> The power came back at about twenty to ten. Nobody switched the LED strings on again for a long time, because the diyas were still burning and nobody wanted to break the spell. I understood that "light over darkness" is not about decoration but about neighbours who refuse to sit in the dark alone and share whatever light they have.
>
> In 2025 UNESCO added Deepavali to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage, a list of traditions that families pass down. For me, that heritage sounds like my grandfather's voice in a dark room full of small flames. This Diwali, I plan to light the first diya myself before anyone touches a single switch.

The UNESCO line is sourced: [decision 20.COM 7.b.24](https://ich.unesco.org/en/decisions/20.COM/7.b.24) inscribed Deepavali in December 2025. It notes that elders pass the festival to children "through stories and hands-on participation", the scene this essay describes.

## The three models side by side: words, paragraphs and focus

Words are counted by plain spaces, as most teachers count by hand. Only Model 3 carries facts, because its turning point needs context.

| Model | Exact words | Paragraphs | The one moment it zooms in on | Checkable fact | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model 1 | 150 | 4 | Guarding one diya on the staircase | None | Classes 3–5 |
| Model 2 | 250 | 5 | Carrying six plates of sweets to neighbours | None | Classes 6–8 |
| Model 3 | 400 | 7 | A power cut at about 7 pm during the puja | Rama's 14-year exile; UNESCO, 2025 | Classes 9–10 |

## Five structure moves, from the 2016 What Works Clearinghouse guide

The [What Works Clearinghouse guide for grades 6–12 (NCEE 2017-4002, November 2016)](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/Docs/PracticeGuide/wwc_secondary_writing_110116.pdf) rates a Model-Practice-Reflect cycle at "strong evidence": the teacher models a strategy, students practise it, then students evaluate their own writing. These are the features to borrow from the models:

- **Answer the title in sentence one.** Name Diwali, then the part you mean.
- **Choose one scene.** One evening told closely beats five days told quickly.
- **Give "I" a job.** Each writer lights, carries or fetches something, so the essay moves.
- **Let someone else speak.** A neighbour's remark adds a second voice cheaply.
- **End on what changed in you.** Close with what you now plan to do this Diwali.

## Check the date before you write "this Diwali"

On 22 October 2026 the top-ranked sample for this search still said Diwali "will be celebrated on October 20, 2025". [Drik Panchang's Lakshmi Puja 2027 timings](https://www.drikpanchang.com/festivals/lakshmipuja/festivals-lakshmipuja-timings.html?year=2027) give Friday, 29 October 2027, muhurat 6:34 pm to 7:05 pm in New Delhi, and Sunday, 8 November for 2026.

Tamil Nadu differs: Drik Panchang lists Tamil Deepavali on Thursday, 28 October 2027, while some holiday lists show 29 October. Check your school calendar.

## Making a model your own in 20 minutes

Spend 5 minutes listing three Diwali moments and circle the one with a surprise. Spend 10 minutes drafting it in first person, then 5 minutes cutting any sentence that could sit in anybody's essay. Reread it the next day if you can: our 2.5-hour revision median comes from greeting pages, not essays, but a draft read again later usually gets sharper.

## Where SubhSandesh fits, and where it does not

SubhSandesh is not an essay tool and will not write or check your essay. Once the essay is done, though, the grandparent in Model 3 may deserve a greeting.

[SubhSandesh's interactive Diwali card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-diwali) puts a wish on each diya, up to six photos in sky lanterns and a letter in a shagun liffafa, in about 5 minutes, as a private link with no app. Send it early: in Raksha Bandhan 2026, our nearest analogue (n = 89), 49.4% of pages were built on the day itself.

If your essay ends with a plan for next Diwali, [the Capsule template](https://subhsandesh.in/capsule) fits better: two people write predictions about the coming year and open them together a year later. It is not a Diwali page and suits two people, such as you and a sibling.

## Sources

- What Works Clearinghouse, *Teaching Secondary Students to Write Effectively*, November 2016.
- von Koss Torkildsen and colleagues, *Reading and Writing* 29: 529–554, 2016 (abstract read).
- UNESCO, decision 20.COM 7.b.24, *Deepavali*, December 2025.
- Drik Panchang, *Lakshmi Puja 2027*: date reference, undated.

structuralLimitations: SERP: India order from DuckDuckGo HTML (lower confidence); WebSearch is US-only. Positions 6–10 not fetched.

The 150/250/400-word sample format is the SERP's table stake (all 5 fetched pages print essays by length). The difference is first-person single-scene recounts at exact stated counts, labelled as models, plus sourced structure tips — not the format.

The Reading and Writing study (PMC4761367, Springer, CC BY) was read as an abstract only; it studied third graders typing stories (keystroke logging), not Indian pupils writing by hand, and the body says it is a pointer not proof. An MDPI recount-writing RCT (Behavioral Sciences PMC12837566) was considered and dropped because MDPI already appears in 3 b2 posts.

The model essays' neighbours, sweets and power cut are invented for the models and the post says so; the essays are original and were written for this post (no sentence or structure reused from b1 diwali-essay, b2 diwali-essay-in-hindi, essay-on-eco-friendly-diwali or 10-lines-on-diwali).
Jain (Mahavira's nirvana) and Sikh (Bandi Chhor Divas) lines in one FAQ are common knowledge stated without a link here; b1 diwali-essay cites primary texts for them.

Tamil Nadu: drikpanchang lists Tamil Deepavali on Thu 28 Oct 2027 vs Lakshmi Puja 29 Oct; the post states the conflict. The 'some state holiday lists show 29 October' clause rests on BRIEF §1 (batch 1 finding); I did not fetch a holiday list myself.

First-party facts are platform-wide (revision gap sampled on /apology-dashboard, publish rate) and the Raksha Bandhan 2026 analogue (n = 89), all labelled; none measures essays or Diwali. The revision-gap figure is used only as an analogy for rereading a draft, and the body says it comes from greeting pages, not essays.

ich.unesco.org: the Deepavali element URL is at its 2-post cap; this post cites a different URL on that host (the 20.COM 7.b.24 decision page), which takes the domain to 3 posts — the domain is now at cap.
Paragraphs: the model essays are blockquoted copyable text; their paragraphs were nonetheless kept to 2–3 sentences. The bold label line above each essay is a caption, not a paragraph.
